The review could not pool any clinical feature: the studies had no consistent measures of clinical characteristics, so its meta-analyses were limited to sex, age and the share of methamphetamine-positive attendees. Its inclusion criteria admitted studies of methamphetamine and related amphetamines (p. 2). The authors list problems with the chart reviews in identifying use, its pattern and frequency, the type of methamphetamine and other drug use, and with self-report; three included studies counted cocaine or other stimulant use; positive urine toxicology likely includes other amphetamine-like compounds and stays positive for 72 hours, which makes it difficult to link use to the presentation; time of last use was not accurately assessed. Two sets of included studies are linked to the same data, and Table 1 lists the acute coronary syndrome study with 171 subjects, against 36 in the text. No deaths or case fatality are reported anywhere in the review's results.

The authors conclude that methamphetamine use is an independent risk factor for violence, but state that they could not be sure of the order of use and violence within each interview period, which limited causal inference; that use and violence were self-reported and not corroborated; and that most people who used did not engage in or experience violence. Of other substances, only alcohol and cannabis use disorders were adjusted for, not other illicit drug use. Ecstasy, analysed the same way, showed no statistically significant adjusted association with any of the four outcomes (all p > 0.05; the authors call the evidence inconclusive); its estimates are only in a supplement.
